line: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4
teaches: When the enemy queen sits on a square your pawn wants, take the square. A developing move that also gains time on the queen is the cheapest tempo in the opening.
explains: The queen took back in the centre and now the pawn takes the square it was standing over, hitting c5 on the way. White has the ideal setup — a broad centre backed by the pawn on c3 — and has not spent a move that was not also useful. Recapturing with the queen is not careless: the chase is short and Black develops during it. This exact position has been reached thousands of times and is deep theory on both sides.

line: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6
teaches: When the queen is exposed, develop a piece that shares its duties. The knight that covers the squares the queen is standing on is worth more than the knight that only looks active.
explains: The knight comes out to f6, the main move by a distance. It contests e4, it takes part in the fight for the centre, and it prepares to castle so the queen is not the only thing keeping the position together. Everything up to here is theory; the branching starts one move from now.

line: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3
teaches: With a broad centre, develop the pieces that hold it. A knight that both comes out and defends the pawn it stands behind never has to be recalled.
explains: The knight comes to f3, adding a guard to d4 as it develops. This is where Black stands at a real crossroads — four different moves here are all worth serious attention, and they lead to genuinely different games rather than transpositions of one another.

line: e4 c5 c3 d5 exd5 Qxd5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 e6
teaches: Between two developing moves, prefer the one that unlocks a piece with no other route. The natural knight move is worse than it looks when it leaves a bishop behind its own pawn.
explains: The pawn steps to e6, which looks like the least ambitious move on the board and is not. The intuitive alternative, bringing the queen's knight out, leaves the dark-squared bishop shut in with nothing to do; this clears its diagonal instead. Developing the light-squared bishop outside the chain is the other serious try. White's answer is the knight round to a3, heading for b5 where it hits c7 and forks the king and rook if allowed, so Black spends a move guarding that square — the queen stepping home or the other knight coming to a6.
